blueprint.speaker: Imogen Tarrow, a former volunteer maintainer of a small text-parsing library for nine years, now writing criticism for a general-interest quarterly
blueprint.audience: Educated general readers of a literary and ideas quarterly, most of whom use software built on volunteer-maintained libraries without knowing it, including managers and engineers at the institutions that depend on such code
blueprint.exigence: The publication of Desmond Alcock's book Nobody's Job, which opens with the recent collapse of thousands of websites after the lone maintainer of the tidyclock library deleted it
blueprint.purpose: To recommend the book's diagnosis of fragile volunteer infrastructure while rejecting its prescribed cure of corporate sponsorship, and to propose instead that dependent institutions contribute maintenance labor
blueprint.context: A review essay in The Harrowgate Quarterly, written shortly after a widely noticed outage caused by a single volunteer quitting
blueprint.claim: Alcock is right that critical software rests on unseen, unpaid individuals, but wrong that money is the remedy; the obligation to maintain should attach to dependence and be paid in hours by the institutions that rely on the code.
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 opens with the tidyclock anecdote and establishes the reviewer's ethos as a former maintainer. Paragraph 2 endorses the book's diagnosis (survey, load-bearing-walls metaphor). Paragraph 3 pivots to the book's prescription, concedes that money has helped, then rebuts with the shoveling analogy: payment converts a gift into a contract. Paragraph 4 shifts to personal testimony about ungrateful bug reports to show that the real deficit is recognition, not cash, and links that back to the critique. Paragraph 5 supplies the alternative cure (institutions lending hours, volunteer fire department analogy) with a qualification of its limits. Paragraph 6 renders the verdict and returns to the schoolteacher of the opening.

devices.function: Opens with the concrete tidyclock collapse to dramatize the stakes and introduce the book's starting point
Establishes the reviewer's standing as a former maintainer who reads the book from inside the problem
Reports Alcock's survey finding to support the diagnosis that most heavily used packages depend on one volunteer
Load-bearing walls figure the hidden, unexamined dependence of institutions on volunteer code; returned to in the proposal to spread the weight
Colons set up the explanation of the metaphor and the statement of Alcock's remedy
Very short sentences after long ones isolate key points: no one chose the arrangement; only one thank-you
Shift from appreciative to critical at paragraph 3, then from analytical to personal and wry at paragraph 4
Grants that stipends have saved projects before rebutting that payment changes the nature of the work
Shoveling the shared walkway shows how payment converts a gift into a service; volunteer fire departments model obligation attached to dependence
Gift versus contract, hours versus dollars, frighten versus comfort sharpen the reviewer's distinctions
Presses readers to recognize that they may have treated a person as a department
The one-word sentence One. wryly registers the scarcity of gratitude without complaint
Limits the proposal's scope so it cannot be dismissed as a cure-all
Instructs the reader how to read the book, delivering the verdict
Parallel clauses build the consequences of payment and balance the two halves of the verdict

blueprint.counterargument: Alcock's position, and the reviewer's own concession, that corporate sponsorship money has in fact rescued projects such as an encryption library; the reviewer grants this and rebuts that payment turns a gift into a contract shaped by the sponsor's priorities.

provenance.note: Original review essay of a fictional book, Nobody's Job, by the fictional author Desmond Alcock. All people, institutions, libraries and figures are invented.

set.title: Standing on Her Work
paragraphs: One Tuesday last October, a date-formatting library called tidyclock vanished from the public package registry, and by morning several thousand websites could no longer tell their users what day it was.
Its sole maintainer, a retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor, had deleted it after a decade of unpaid work and one rude bug report too many.
Desmond Alcock's new book, Nobody's Job, opens with that night, and it is the right place to begin.
I spent nine years maintaining a small text-parsing library used by companies I was never allowed to name, so I read Alcock with the uneasy attention of a patient reading her own chart.
The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one.
Alcock surveyed four hundred of the most heavily downloaded packages in three programming languages and found that more than half depended on a single active volunteer.

He calls these projects load-bearing walls that no inspector has visited, and the metaphor earns its keep: the walls are hidden inside the plaster of every bank, hospital, and school district that runs code on top of them.
Nobody chose this arrangement.
It accreted, one convenient download at a time, until the whole structure rested on the patience of people who could stop at any moment and owed us nothing if they did.
It is in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure, that the book loses its footing.
His remedy is sponsorship: corporations that profit from open-source software should fund its maintainers, and he describes several foundations that already do so.
I will grant that money has saved projects.
A stipend kept at least one widely used encryption library alive after its maintainer nearly quit, and Alcock tells that story well.
But a stipend changes what the work is.

Consider the neighbor who shovels the shared walkway every winter because no one else will; the day you start paying her, the shoveling becomes a service, the snow becomes her problem, and you acquire the right to complain about ice.
Sponsorship converts a gift into a contract, and the contract arrives written in the sponsor's priorities, not the project's.
I know something about how such gifts are received.

In nine years I received roughly four thousand bug reports, most of them phrased as demands, several of them threatening, and one, from a hospital network in a city I have never visited, that began with the words "thank you."
One.
Did any of those four thousand correspondents imagine that a person, rather than a department, was reading them at eleven at night?
Alcock understands this loneliness better than any writer I have read, which is precisely why his faith in a check is so puzzling.
The better cure is already visible in the margins of his own book, though he never names it.
The institutions that depend on these libraries do not lack money; they lack a sense that the maintenance is theirs to do.
A regional bank runs tidyclock on its login page, employs ninety engineers, and has never assigned one of them a Friday afternoon to review tidyclock's open issues.
Volunteer fire departments survive not because the town mails a check to the one person who owns a hose but because the people whose houses would burn show up for the drills.
The obligation should attach to dependence, not to profit, and it should be paid in hours, not dollars.
This will not rescue every project, and the smallest libraries will still rely on the stubbornness of individuals; but it would spread the weight across the walls that bear it.
Nobody's Job deserves the wide readership it will probably get.
Read it for the first half, which will frighten you in the right way, and argue with the second, which will comfort you in the wrong one.
The retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor did not need a sponsor.
She needed the several thousand of us who were standing on her work to notice that we were.

items.stem: The writer's account in paragraph 4 of the bug reports she received over nine years is most likely intended to affect readers by

options.text: prompting them to recognize that they, too, may have treated an individual volunteer as if she were an anonymous department
options.label: correct
options.why: The account of demanding reports is followed by a question asking whether any correspondent imagined 'a person, rather than a department' was reading them, and the essay closes by naming 'the several thousand of us who were standing on her work'; the audience of ordinary users is being implicated in the neglect.

options.text: demonstrating that hospital networks are more considerate users of volunteer code than banks or corporations
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The single hospital thank-you is used as a rarity, not as a comparison among institutional types; the passage never ranks hospitals against banks.

options.text: establishing the technical authority she needs to challenge the findings of Alcock's survey
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: She does not challenge the survey; she endorses the diagnosis in paragraph 2. The anecdote concerns recognition and loneliness, not technical credentials.

options.text: suggesting that maintainers are too easily wounded to be trusted with critical infrastructure
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage's sympathy runs toward maintainers and against those who make demands of them; it faults the dependents, not the volunteers.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the sentence beginning "A stipend kept at least one widely used encryption library alive" functions primarily as

options.text: evidence supporting the writer's concession that sponsorship money has in fact rescued some projects
options.label: correct
options.why: It directly follows 'I will grant that money has saved projects' and supplies a specific case of a stipend saving a library, before the rebuttal 'But a stipend changes what the work is.'

options.text: evidence supporting the writer's claim that obligations should be paid in hours rather than dollars
options.label: reversal
options.why: The example shows money working, which is the opposite of the hours-not-dollars claim; it belongs to the conceded point, not the writer's own remedy.

options.text: a claim that Alcock's survey of four hundred packages underestimates the role of foundations
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence reports a specific case rather than asserting a general position, and it says nothing about the survey's accuracy.

options.text: evidence that the second half of the book is better written than the first
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Although the writer notes Alcock 'tells that story well,' she has just said the second half 'loses its footing' and never compares the prose quality of the two halves.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the writer's acknowledgment that her proposal "will not rescue every project" chiefly strengthens the argument by

options.text: limiting the proposal to a realistic scope, so that it avoids the overconfidence she has just criticized in Alcock's cure
options.label: correct
options.why: Having faulted Alcock's 'faith in a check' and called his cure comforting 'in the wrong' way, the writer narrows her own claim before the semicolon and then affirms its real benefit, spreading the weight across the walls; the qualification makes her remedy harder to dismiss as a cure-all.

options.text: conceding that the smallest libraries will still require corporate sponsorship after all
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The sentence says the smallest libraries will rely on 'the stubbornness of individuals,' not on sponsorship; the passage never readmits Alcock's remedy.

options.text: shifting the burden of the solution back onto individual maintainers rather than institutions
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The clause about individuals describes a residual limit, while the main thrust of the paragraph remains the institutions' duty; the qualification does not relocate the burden.

options.text: admitting that the fire department analogy ultimately fails to apply to software
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Nothing in the sentence retracts the analogy; it follows the hours-not-dollars claim and ends by reaffirming the proposal's benefit with the load-bearing-walls image.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3?

options.text: Paragraph 2 endorses the book's diagnosis of the problem, and paragraph 3 rejects the book's proposed cure
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 2 opens 'The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one,' and paragraph 3 opens by locating the book's failure 'in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure.'

options.text: Paragraph 2 raises a problem, and paragraph 3 presents the writer's own solution to it
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Paragraph 3 examines and rebuts Alcock's solution; the writer's own solution does not appear until paragraph 5.

options.text: Paragraph 2 praises the book's survey, and paragraph 3 shows that the survey's findings were flawed
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer never questions the survey; she continues to accept the diagnosis and later says the first half 'will frighten you in the right way.'

options.text: Paragraph 2 states the writer's thesis, and paragraph 3 supplies evidence supporting it
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Paragraph 2 summarizes Alcock's findings rather than the writer's thesis, and paragraph 3 turns against the book rather than supporting what precedes it.

items.stem: The sentence "Alcock understands this loneliness better than any writer I have read, which is precisely why his faith in a check is so puzzling" primarily serves to

options.text: return the personal testimony of paragraph 4 to the evaluation of the book by tying the lack of recognition to the inadequacy of sponsorship
options.label: correct
options.why: After the digression into her own bug reports, the sentence names Alcock again and uses 'this loneliness' to connect the anecdote's point about being unseen to the critique that money cannot address it, preparing the alternative cure in paragraph 5.

options.text: soften the review's criticism by conceding that Alcock's empathy outweighs the weakness of his remedy
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The praise of Alcock's understanding is real, but the sentence uses it to sharpen, not soften, the objection: his insight makes the remedy 'puzzling.'

options.text: introduce the writer's proposal that institutions should contribute engineers' hours instead of money
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The proposal is introduced in the next paragraph with 'The better cure is already visible'; this sentence only diagnoses the mismatch in Alcock's thinking.

options.text: convey the writer's contempt for a critic who has never maintained software himself
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence credits Alcock with unmatched understanding; its tone is puzzled and respectful, and the passage never says Alcock lacks maintenance experience.

items.stem: The effect of the one-word sentence "One." in paragraph 4 is best described as

options.text: isolating the number with wry understatement so that the rarity of gratitude registers more sharply than any complaint could
options.label: correct
options.why: The word follows a long sentence cataloguing four thousand demanding reports; its brevity sets the single thank-you apart, and the flat restatement without commentary is understated rather than indignant.

options.text: expressing open anger at the hospital network that waited so long to thank her
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The hospital is the one correspondent who did thank her; the passage directs no anger at it, and the restraint of a single word is the opposite of open anger.

options.text: establishing the writer's credibility by showing she kept precise records of every report
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The passage says 'roughly four thousand,' signalling approximation; the short sentence is about scarcity of thanks, not record-keeping.

options.text: emphasizing that only one institution was actually using the writer's library
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The 'one' counts thank-you messages, not users; the previous sentence establishes thousands of correspondents, and paragraph 1 refers to companies she could not name.

the economics of free public parks

blueprint.purpose: A student council proposal urging the town parks commission to reject a proposed entry fee at a public park and to adopt a student volunteer maintenance crew instead
blueprint.audience: The Halvering Parks Commission, a board of adult appointees focused on budgets, reliability, and liability
blueprint.claim: A free Brindle Creek Park is a better economic choice for Halvering than a 3-dollar entry fee because the fee would raise less than projected and student volunteers can cut maintenance costs
blueprint.theme: the economics of free public parks
blueprint.speaker: Dario Velloso-Krantz, treasurer of the Halvering High student council
blueprint.exigence: The Halvering Parks Commission has announced it is considering an entry fee to cover a maintenance shortfall and will vote at its May meeting
blueprint.context: A written proposal submitted to the commission before its May vote, drawing on a council-run survey, a local business owner's testimony, and the commission's own cost report
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Occasion and request; the fee would collect less than projected because attendance would fall and nearby shops would suffer; a volunteer crew could remove 17,000 dollars of contractor costs; closing appeal to the park's role in town life
blueprint.counterargument: The commission needs 41,000 dollars and a fee seems like the straightforward way to get it; volunteer programs are often unreliable
evidence_types: testimony from a local business owner
precedent of the fall cleanup event

devices.function: The repeated 'where' clauses accumulate the park's everyday uses to show what the fee would put at risk
'First' and 'Second' mark the two economic arguments of the proposal

tone_shifts.to: flippant and dismissive, a mismatch for the commission

planned_flaws.flaw: Vague, generic opening that does not establish the occasion or stakes
planned_flaws.repair_type: replace opening sentence with a concrete scene tied to the draft's details

planned_flaws.flaw: Thesis is vague, does not require proof, and does not preview the two-part structure
planned_flaws.repair_type: replace with an arguable, structured thesis

planned_flaws.flaw: Survey evidence is presented without commentary linking it to the claim in sentence 5
Sentence about the commission's attendance projection is misplaced after the bakery detail, breaking the chain of reasoning
Unsupported assurance that ignores the commission's known concern about volunteer reliability
planned_flaws.repair_type: revise to address the audience's concern with a concrete accountability mechanism

planned_flaws.flaw: Colloquial, dismissive wording ('a pretty dumb move') mismatched to a formal proposal
planned_flaws.repair_type: replace phrase with confident but respectful wording

provenance.venue_alias: Halvering High Student Council proposal to the Halvering Parks Commission
provenance.note: Entirely fictional town, commission, school, business, survey, and figures invented for practice purposes.

set.title: Proposal to Keep Brindle Creek Park Free
paragraphs: Parks are something that most people have an opinion about.
Last month the Halvering Parks Commission announced that it is considering a 3-dollar entry fee at Brindle Creek Park to cover a 41,000-dollar maintenance shortfall.
As treasurer of the Halvering High student council, I am writing on behalf of our 38 members to ask the commission to vote against the fee at its May meeting.
Free parks are good for Halvering in a lot of ways.
First, the fee would raise less money than it appears to.
Our council surveyed 212 students and parents outside the park gate on two Saturdays in April.
Sixty-four percent said they would visit less often if the fee were adopted, and 29 percent said they would stop coming altogether.
Fewer visitors would also mean fewer customers on Kettle Street, where the owner of Marron's Bakery told us that weekend park traffic brings in roughly a third of her sales.
The commission's projection counts on 60,000 paid entries a year, but that figure assumes attendance stays flat.
Second, a free park can be cheaper to maintain than the commission's numbers suggest.
Our council already organizes a fall cleanup that drew 90 volunteers last October.
We propose expanding it into a monthly Saturday crew, supervised by parks staff, that handles litter pickup, mulching, and repainting the picnic shelters.
The commission's own report prices those three tasks at 17,000 dollars a year in contractor costs.
Students love being outside, so they will definitely show up.
Turning down that much free labor would be a pretty dumb move.
Brindle Creek Park is where the cross-country team trains, where the kindergarten classes count ducks, and where my grandfather plays chess on Thursdays.
We ask the commission to keep the gate open and to let us help pay for it with our Saturdays.
Thank you for considering this proposal.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 1 with an opening sentence that presents a concrete scene showing what is at stake in the commission's vote and that is consistent with the details given later in the draft. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: On a warm Saturday in April, the picnic shelters at Brindle Creek Park fill before ten in the morning with families who did not pay a cent to be there.
options.label: correct
options.why: It opens with a specific scene at the park, highlights the free access that the fee would end, and matches later details such as the April survey Saturdays and the picnic shelters.

options.text: Across the country, towns of every size have debated whether public parks should charge visitors for entry.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It is a generalization about towns everywhere rather than a concrete scene at Brindle Creek Park, so it does not show what is at stake locally.

options.text: Most weekends, Brindle Creek Park sits nearly empty, its picnic shelters peeling and its paths littered with trash no one bothers to collect.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It presents a scene that contradicts the draft, which describes heavy weekend traffic, 90 cleanup volunteers, and a park central to town life.

options.text: The commission should reject the entry fee because the fee would raise less than expected and volunteers could reduce costs.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It states the argument's thesis rather than presenting a scene, so it does not accomplish the writer's stated goal for the opening.

items.stem: The writer has learned that commission members have said in past meetings that volunteer programs tend to fade after a few months. The writer wants to revise sentence 14 so that it directly addresses this concern. Which version of sentence 14 best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: To keep the crew from fading, the council will collect signed semester commitments from each member and send the commission an attendance report after every work day.
options.label: correct
options.why: It names the commission's specific worry and offers concrete accountability measures, which suits an audience focused on reliability and oversight.

options.text: Students love being outside, and a Saturday at the park beats a Saturday on the couch.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It appeals to student enjoyment in casual language and offers the commission no assurance about sustained participation.

options.text: Volunteer programs have revitalized public parks in cities across the country.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It asserts a sweeping claim with no evidence in the draft and does not address whether this particular crew would last.

options.text: Our fall cleanup shows that Halvering students care deeply about Brindle Creek Park.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: It cites relevant evidence of enthusiasm, but a single October event does not answer the concern that participation will fade over months.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 4 with a thesis statement that makes a claim requiring proof and that previews the structure of the second and third paragraphs. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The fee would collect far less than the commission expects, and a student volunteer crew could close much of the shortfall at no cost to the town.
options.label: correct
options.why: It makes a debatable claim and lays out the two supporting arguments in the order the draft develops them in paragraphs two and three.

options.text: Free public parks are important to communities everywhere, no matter their size.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It is a general statement that does not require specific proof and says nothing about the fee, the survey, or the volunteer plan.

options.text: Brindle Creek Park has been free since it opened and contains a pond, a creek, and six picnic shelters.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It is a description of facts rather than an arguable claim, so it cannot serve as a thesis that the body must prove.

options.text: The commission should reject the fee because charging students to use a park they already help maintain is unfair.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: It is arguable, but its fairness argument does not match the economic reasoning of the body and does not preview the two-part structure.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that explains how the survey results support the claim made in sentence 5. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: If even half of those respondents followed through, the commission would be collecting fees from a crowd far smaller than the one it has counted on.
options.label: correct
options.why: It connects the attendance drop in the survey to the revenue claim in sentence 5 by showing that fewer visitors means fewer fees collected.

options.text: In other words, nearly two thirds of the people we spoke with planned to come less often, and almost a third planned to stop entirely.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It merely restates the figures from sentence 7 instead of explaining what they mean for the fee's revenue.

options.text: These results prove that the fee would fail completely and leave the commission with no revenue at all.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It overstates the evidence; a survey of 212 people cannot establish that the fee would collect nothing.

options.text: The results also show that families in Halvering simply cannot afford to pay 3 dollars to enter a park.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: It shifts from the revenue argument of sentence 5 to a claim about affordability that the survey did not measure.

items.stem: The writer wants to reorder paragraph 2 so that the reasoning moves from the commission's revenue assumption to the evidence that challenges it. Where should sentence 9 be placed to best accomplish this goal?

options.text: Immediately after sentence 5
options.label: correct
options.why: Placed after the claim, sentence 9 states the flat-attendance assumption, and the survey in sentences 6 and 7 then directly challenges it before sentence 8 extends the effects to local shops.

options.text: Where it is now, after sentence 8
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Left in place, the sentence jumps back to the attendance projection after the paragraph has already moved on to the bakery's sales, breaking the chain of reasoning.

options.text: Most weekends, Brindle Creek Park sits nearly empty, its picnic shelters peeling and its paths littered with trash no one bothers to collect.

options.text: Students love being outside, and a Saturday at the park beats a Saturday on the couch.

options.text: Our fall cleanup shows that Halvering students care deeply about Brindle Creek Park.

options.text: To keep the crew from fading, the council will collect signed semester commitments from each member and send the commission an attendance report after every work day.

blueprint.purpose: A year-end report from a student team captain to the school's Student Activities Board, which will vote on whether to fund the robotics club for a second year
blueprint.audience: The Harlow Creek High School Student Activities Board: a faculty-and-student committee that allocates club budgets and values participation, learning outcomes, and careful use of money
blueprint.claim: In its first season the Gearhounds built a working robot, turned beginners into capable builders, and need only modest funding to continue
blueprint.genre: report on a school project draft
blueprint.theme: the first season of a school robotics team
blueprint.speaker: Teodor Vasquez-Lindqvist, a tenth grader and captain of the Gearhounds robotics team
blueprint.exigence: The Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before its budget vote
blueprint.context: The team began in August in the woodshop with donated equipment and competed in April at the fictional Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Narrative opening establishes starting point and result; paragraph 2 traces the build process and a solved problem; paragraph 3 asserts learning and attendance; paragraph 4 lists needs and closes with a plea
blueprint.counterargument: Not addressed in the draft; the board might see a new club as an unproven expense

devices.function: Frames the season as a before-and-after story to make the result vivid
Shows the sequence of the build so the board can see steady progress
Links a failure to a diagnosed cause to show problem-solving
Contrasts a large request with a small one to make the ask seem modest

planned_flaws.flaw: Vague thesis that makes no claim and does not preview the report's organization
planned_flaws.repair_type: replace with a thesis that requires proof and previews three sections

planned_flaws.flaw: Casual, slangy wording inappropriate for a formal report to a budget committee
Claim that members learned a great deal is asserted without specific evidence
planned_flaws.repair_type: add a sentence with concrete evidence of learning

planned_flaws.flaw: Comma splice joining two independent clauses
Appeal rests on popularity and bravado rather than on values the board holds (participation, learning, frugality)
Problem-solving moment lacks a comparison that would make the team's method clear to non-engineers

set.title: The Gearhounds: A First-Season Report
paragraphs: Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot.
Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore.
This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened.
I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.
The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting.
Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left.
Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon.
By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required.
Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.
The members learned a great deal from the season.
Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.
Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration.
The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it.
We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 14 so that its reason for funding appeals to the values of the Student Activities Board, which sentence 4 identifies as the committee that votes on club budgets. Which version of sentence 14 best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The board should fund us because the team kept eleven students meeting every week for eight months using nothing but donated and secondhand equipment.
options.label: correct
options.why: Appeals to what a budget committee values, sustained participation and frugal use of resources, and both details are supported by sentences 1 and 12.

options.text: The board should fund us because robotics is the coolest club around, and the board members would agree if they ever stopped by the woodshop.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Keeps the boastful, casual appeal to popularity and adds a mild jab at the board, which does not match a formal budget report.

options.text: The board should fund us because every member plans to major in engineering and will credit the school for that choice.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Introduces a sweeping claim about members' future plans that nothing in the report supports.

options.text: The board should fund us because Marmalade's orange zip ties made it the most memorable robot at the competition in Dunmore.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Rests the case on the robot's appearance, a detail that does not speak to participation, learning, or cost, the concerns of a budget committee.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that provides specific evidence for the claim that the members learned a great deal during the season. Which sentence best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Two members who could not define a gear ratio in September wrote the technical notebook that the judges scored in April.
options.label: correct
options.why: Gives a concrete before-and-after example of skill growth in named terms that directly supports the claim about learning.

options.text: The season was long and demanding, and members gave up many Saturdays to keep working on Marmalade.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Offers evidence of effort and commitment, not of what members learned, so it supports a different claim.

options.text: Research consistently shows that hands-on clubs teach students more than classroom lectures do.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a generic claim about clubs in general with no source and says nothing about these particular members.

options.text: Learning a great deal is the main reason any club deserves the school's financial support.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Functions as commentary about why learning matters rather than as evidence that learning occurred.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a thesis statement that makes a claim the report must support and previews the organization of the three body paragraphs. Which version best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: In its first season the Gearhounds built a working robot, turned beginners into capable builders, and identified exactly what the team needs to continue, as the three sections below show.
options.label: correct
options.why: Asserts three claims that require proof and maps them, in order, onto paragraphs 2, 3, and 4.

options.text: Robotics teams everywhere face the same challenges in their first season, and ours was no exception.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Makes a generalization about all teams that the report never addresses and previews none of its sections.

options.text: This report describes the team's meetings, the robot's design, and the competition in Dunmore.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Announces topics without making an arguable claim, and the listed topics do not match the actual paragraphs.

options.text: The Gearhounds proved that a first-year team can place in the top ten at the Tri-County Build Challenge.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: States a claim that needs proof but covers only the competition result and gives no preview of the report's structure.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that uses a comparison to help board members unfamiliar with engineering understand the team's approach, and that advances the argument that the team learned to solve problems efficiently. Which sentence best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Like a mechanic who checks the tires before rebuilding the engine, we had learned to look for the simplest explanation first.
options.label: correct
options.why: Offers a familiar analogy that clarifies the method in sentence 7 and frames it as a learned, efficient habit.

options.text: A mismatched wheel pair is a common error in beginner builds, according to the instruction booklet that came with the kit.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Explains the error rather than comparing the approach, and shifts attention to the mistake instead of the problem-solving.

options.text: Like a team that forfeits rather than finishes, we knew that quitting was always an option.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The comparison contradicts sentence 7, which shows the team persisting, and undercuts the argument about efficient problem-solving.

options.text: Robots, like people, have good days and bad days, and November was a bad month for Marmalade.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Has the form of a comparison but says nothing about how the team diagnosed or fixed the problem.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 9 so that it reports the judges' reaction in a tone appropriate for a formal report to the Student Activities Board without overstating what happened. Which version best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Two of the judges told our adviser that they had not expected a first-year team to arrive with a fully functioning robot.
options.label: correct
options.why: Uses measured, specific wording suited to a formal report and attributes the reaction to particular judges without exaggeration.

options.text: Honestly, the judges were pretty shocked that a rookie team even pulled off a working bot.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Retains the casual, conversational register of the original, including slang like 'pulled off' and 'bot.'

options.text: The adjudicating personnel expressed considerable astonishment regarding the operational status of our apparatus.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Swings to inflated, stilted diction that sounds pompous and does not match the plain voice of the rest of the report.

options.text: Every judge at the competition agreed that Marmalade was the most impressive robot of the day.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Replaces the casual tone with a claim the writer cannot support, especially given the ninth-place finish in sentence 2.

items.stem: The writer wants to correct the punctuation of sentence 11 so that its two independent clauses are properly joined while the original meaning is preserved. Which version accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before; by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
options.label: correct
options.why: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses and keeps 'by March' attached to the teaching.

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, however, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A conjunctive adverb set off by commas cannot join two independent clauses; the comma splice remains.

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before by March, they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Moves 'by March' to the first clause, changing the meaning, and still leaves a comma splice.

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March, they were teaching the eighth graders, who visited on shadow day.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Adds commas but never supplies a semicolon or coordinating conjunction, so the two clauses are still spliced.
